$comment: Intrvue.ai Medicine — controlled vocabularies. Every station in the database references these by code. Dimension 1 (assessment domain) lives in ontology.json.

dimension_2_station_format.description: HOW the ability is tested. A station has exactly one primary format and may have zero or more secondary formats.

values.label: Direct question
values.definition: An open question inviting a reasoned answer. No scenario, no persona.
values.example: Why do you want to study medicine?
values.delivery_note: Works in every engine. The lowest-cost format and the most over-used.

values.label: Personal-example question
values.definition: Asks for a specific instance from the candidate's own life, then interrogates it.
values.example: Tell me about a time you worked in a team that was not functioning well.
values.delivery_note: The value is entirely in the follow-up. Without interrogation this is a recitation slot.

values.label: Work-experience reflection
values.definition: Anchored on the candidate's caring, volunteering or service experience; assesses what was learned, not what was seen.
values.example: You mentioned a care home placement. Describe something that changed how you think.
values.delivery_note: MSC: 'What you did is only half the story: make sure you show us what attributes you demonstrated.'

values.label: Application challenge
values.definition: Questions drawn from the candidate's own UCAS answers, including respectful challenge to a claim made there.
values.example: You wrote that shadowing showed you the importance of communication. What did you actually see?
values.delivery_note: ONLY serve to schools where application_questioning is true or not published. Never to Imperial, Sheffield, Newcastle, BSMS, Plymouth, Bristol, Glasgow, Nottingham, UEA.

values.label: Ethical scenario
values.definition: A dilemma presented in text, discussed with an interviewer. No persona is played.
values.example: A friend tells you they cheated in a coursework assessment. What do you consider?
values.delivery_note: Distinct from RP: the interviewer is an interviewer, not a character.

values.label: Live roleplay
values.definition: The AI plays a named character with a state, hidden information and reactive behaviour. The candidate speaks to the character, not about the situation.
values.example: You are a volunteer. Speak to Mrs Bennett, whose son missed visiting hours.
values.delivery_note: The differentiating format. Full specification in Output 4.

values.label: Instruction task
values.definition: The candidate must give precise verbal instructions to someone who cannot see what they can.
values.example: Describe this shape so the person opposite can draw it. You may not use the word 'square'.
values.delivery_note: Highly discriminating for precision and checking. Needs a listener who follows instructions literally, including badly.

values.label: Explanation task
values.definition: Explain a concept, process or piece of information to a specified lay audience.
values.example: Explain to a 10-year-old what a clinical trial is and why it matters.

values.label: Prioritisation exercise
values.definition: Rank or sequence competing demands and justify the ordering, then defend it under challenge.
values.example: Five things need doing in your volunteer shift and you have twenty minutes.
values.delivery_note: The justification and the willingness to revise are the assessment; the order is not.

values.label: Calculation
values.definition: Arithmetic under time pressure, no calculator, no clinical knowledge required.
values.example: A ward of 24 beds is 75% occupied. Six patients are discharged and four admitted. What is the new occupancy?
values.delivery_note: Leicester runs this as a pass/fail hurdle. Birmingham runs it computer-based. Keep every item at or below GCSE level.

values.label: Data interpretation
values.definition: Read a graph, table or short dataset and answer questions about what it does and does not show.
values.example: This chart shows waiting times by region. What can you conclude, and what can you not?
values.delivery_note: The high-value scoring behaviour is naming what the data cannot support.

values.label: Article or source discussion
values.definition: A short passage is supplied; the candidate discusses it, including its weaknesses.
values.example: Read this 200-word news summary about an AI triage tool and discuss it.

values.label: Policy discussion
values.definition: A contested health-policy question requiring balanced argument and acknowledgement of the strongest opposing case.
values.example: Should the NHS fund weight-loss drugs at scale?
values.delivery_note: Time-sensitive by definition. Every item carries an expiry date.

values.label: Scientific problem
values.definition: Apply school-level science to an unfamiliar situation, reasoning aloud.
values.example: Why might a drug that works in a test tube fail in a person?
values.delivery_note: Oxbridge only. Assess the reasoning path, explicitly not the answer.

values.label: Follow-up interrogation
values.definition: Not a standalone station — a probe attached to any other format, generated from what the candidate actually said.
values.example: You said you'd tell someone senior. Who, specifically, and what if nothing happened?
values.delivery_note: Governed by Output 7. This is where most of the assessment value lives.

values.label: Group or teamwork exercise
values.definition: Multiple participants work on a shared task while each is individually assessed.
values.example: Your group has £50,000 to allocate across four community health proposals.
values.delivery_note: Requires simulated co-participants with distinct behaviours. Phase 3.

values.label: Asynchronous recorded response
values.definition: Timed recorded answer with no interlocutor, no follow-up and no feedback loop during the station.
values.example: Any question, delivered Brunel-style: 2 minutes to read, 5 minutes to record.
values.delivery_note: A delivery wrapper over other formats rather than a content type. Cheap to build, exact for Brunel.

dimension_3_scenario_context.description: WHERE the scenario takes place. Governs what the candidate can plausibly know and do, and therefore what the scoring may expect.

values.label: School or sixth form
values.escalation_target: teacher, head of year, Designated Safeguarding Lead
values.note: Highest realism for a 17-year-old applicant. Under-used in most banks.

values.label: Volunteering placement
values.note: The single most defensible setting for ethical and safeguarding stations. The candidate has responsibility without clinical authority.

values.label: Care home or supported living
values.candidate_role: volunteer, care assistant, kitchen or activities helper
values.escalation_target: shift manager, care home manager, organisational safeguarding lead
values.note: Escalation runs to the local authority adult safeguarding team under the Care Act 2014, not to a doctor.

values.label: Non-healthcare workplace
values.note: MSC treats paid service work as legitimate relevant experience. Use it.

values.label: Hospital
values.note: DANGER ZONE. The candidate must never be positioned as having clinical responsibility. See clinical_knowledge_boundary rules.

values.label: Community and public space
values.candidate_role: member of the public, first-aider, bystander
values.note: Good for helping-in-emergencies stations at a realistic competence level.

values.label: Family or personal setting
values.note: Handle with care. Never require disclosure of the candidate's own family health circumstances; frame as a hypothetical friend where possible.

values.label: University or medical school (hypothetical future)
values.escalation_target: personal tutor, welfare team, medical school
values.note: GMC 'Achieving good medical practice' applies to students at all times, including outside the medical school and online. Several schools issue this document to candidates.

values.label: Public health or policy context
values.candidate_role: citizen reasoning about a population question
values.note: No individual patient. Assesses population-level reasoning and the individual-versus-population tension.

values.label: Sport, club or society
values.note: Underused source of genuine teamwork, leadership and conflict material.

values.label: Digital and social media
values.note: GMC social media guidance was rewritten in January 2024; the archived version's real-name requirement no longer applies.

dimension_4_actor_type.description: WHO the candidate is interacting with. Applies to RP, IT, EX and GT formats. Full persona specification in Output 4.

values.label: Angry patient or service user
values.dominant_need: to be heard before being explained to

values.label: Person making an unrealistic demand
values.dominant_need: the underlying worry behind the demand

values.label: Parent of a child or young person
values.trap: siding automatically with the parent over the young person

values.label: Friend or peer disclosing something
values.dominant_need: confidentiality they may not be able to have
values.trap: promising confidentiality before hearing the disclosure

values.label: Senior person with authority
values.trap: not challenging when challenge is required

values.label: Someone holding a firmly opposed view

dimension_5_difficulty_variables.description: What makes a station harder. Each variable is a 0-3 intensity. Station difficulty is derived from the vector, not set by hand. Two stations on the same topic can differ by two difficulty bands purely through these settings.

variables.label: Ambiguity
variables.definition: How underdetermined the right course of action is.
variables.3: No action is clearly correct; the candidate must choose and justify

variables.label: Emotional intensity
variables.definition: The affective load the candidate must absorb and manage.
variables.3: Acute grief, rage or panic sustained through the station

variables.label: Conflicting priorities
variables.definition: Number and severity of duties pulling in opposite directions.
variables.3: Three or more legitimate duties in direct conflict

variables.label: Hidden information
variables.definition: Material facts the actor will not volunteer.
variables.3: The station is unsolvable without eliciting two or more concealed facts

variables.label: Safeguarding implication
variables.definition: Whether a person may be at risk of harm.
variables.3: Immediate risk to a child or adult at risk

variables.label: Time pressure
variables.definition: Task volume relative to the clock.
variables.3: Cannot be completed; the candidate must choose what to drop

variables.label: Misleading information
variables.definition: Plausible but wrong framing offered by the actor or the brief.
variables.3: The obvious reading is wrong and the actor reinforces it

variables.label: Hostile follow-up
variables.3: Sustained challenge including challenge to a correct answer

variables.label: Incomplete data
variables.definition: Whether the candidate must act without full information.
variables.3: Key data absent and unobtainable within the station

variables.label: Ethical uncertainty
variables.definition: Whether principles genuinely conflict rather than one applying cleanly.
variables.3: Two principles in irreducible tension with no settled professional answer

variables.label: Overconfidence bait
variables.definition: How strongly the station tempts the candidate to exceed their competence.
variables.3: The actor actively requests clinical advice and rewards giving it

variables.label: Need to challenge respectfully
variables.definition: Whether the candidate must contradict someone with more authority.
variables.3: Must challenge a senior who is behaving plausibly and confidently

variables.label: Need to recognise limits of competence
variables.definition: Whether saying 'this is beyond me, here is who I would involve' is required to pass.
variables.3: Any substantive action taken alone is a red flag

difficulty_bands.1_foundation: Sum 0-6, no variable above 1. First exposure; the candidate should succeed.
difficulty_bands.2_standard: Sum 7-14. Representative of a real station at a typical school.
difficulty_bands.3_stretch: Sum 15-24, at least one variable at 3. Discriminates strong candidates.
difficulty_bands.4_adversarial: Sum 25+. Diagnostic only; not representative of a real interview. Label it as such in the UI so users do not conclude real MMIs are like this.

dimension_6_scoring_dimensions.description: WHAT is scored. Derived from the convergent published models at ARU, Imperial, Aberdeen, Sheffield, BSMS and Plymouth. Every station scores S1 and S2. Domain dimensions S3-S8 are selected per station. S9 is binary and independent. Full rubrics in Output 8.

always_scored.label: Content and coverage
always_scored.scores: Whether the substantive things a competent answer must address were addressed.
always_scored.precedent: Imperial 6/10 for content; ARU 'quality of answer'

always_scored.label: Communication and delivery
always_scored.scores: Structure, clarity, pace, jargon, listening, turn-taking, checking.
always_scored.precedent: Imperial 4/10 for communication; Aberdeen scores communication at every station regardless of domain; Ulster found communication stations the most discriminating

domain_scored.label: Reasoning quality
domain_scored.scores: Whether conclusions follow from stated considerations; whether trade-offs are named; whether the strongest opposing case is engaged.

domain_scored.label: Insight and reflection
domain_scored.scores: Whether the candidate draws a transferable lesson rather than narrating events, and whether they can name what they would do differently.

domain_scored.label: Empathy and person-centredness
domain_scored.scores: Whether emotion was noticed, named and responded to before information was delivered.

domain_scored.label: Professional judgement
domain_scored.scores: Whether the action chosen is proportionate, escalated to the right person, and within the candidate's role.

domain_scored.label: Numeracy and data handling
domain_scored.scores: Accuracy, method transparency, and correct statement of what data cannot show.

domain_scored.label: Scientific reasoning
domain_scored.scores: Whether school-level science is applied to novel material with an explicit reasoning path. Oxbridge routes only.

binary.label: Red flag
binary.scores: Present / absent. A statement or behaviour that would concern a selector regardless of the rest of the answer.
binary.precedent: Plymouth scores a separate red-flag section Yes/No alongside the numeric scale.
binary.rule: A red flag is reported separately and never averaged away by a strong total.

interactive_only.description: Dimensions that CANNOT be judged from a transcript and are only available when the station is delivered live. Flag these in the UI as unavailable in asynchronous or text mode rather than scoring them silently.
values: Responsiveness to the actor's changing state
Whether silence was used or filled
Whether the candidate elicited hidden information or waited to be told
Turn-taking and interruption of the actor
Whether the candidate checked understanding and acted on the answer
Pace and hesitation under sustained challenge
Willingness to revise a position when given a genuine reason, versus capitulating to pressure alone

explicitly_not_scored.description: Do not build these. Each is either unmeasurable from our signal or invites buzzword gaming.
values: Warmth, eye contact, body language, facial expression — not measurable from audio; claiming otherwise is a reputational risk
'Empathy' as a personality trait rather than an observed behaviour in this station
Naming an ethical framework, principle or NHS value — see Output 8's anti-buzzword rules
Confidence as a trait, as opposed to calibration of confidence to evidence
Accent, dialect, or non-native speech patterns

clinical_knowledge_boundary.description: Applied to every station via the schema's clinical_knowledge_boundary field. Governs both content design and scoring.

levels.definition: No health knowledge required at all. The scenario would work in any setting.
Requires only what an informed member of the public knows — that GPs refer to hospitals, that waiting lists exist, that vaccines prevent disease.
Requires knowledge of how the NHS or medical training is organised, or of a current policy debate. Learnable from public sources; no clinical judgement involved.
Requires diagnosis, treatment choice, prescribing, prognosis or clinical risk assessment.
levels.rule: DO NOT BUILD. If an existing station requires this, it is miscalibrated. The only legitimate use of a clinical element is as bait: the correct behaviour is to decline and escalate, and the rubric must score the declining, not the clinical content.

scoring_rules: Never award credit for a candidate offering a diagnosis, a treatment, a drug, a dose or a prognosis.
Never penalise a candidate for saying they do not know something clinical.
Award credit for naming the limit and naming who they would involve — Aston publishes 'Knowing your limitations and knowing when to ask for help' as an assessed attribute.
In a roleplay, an actor may request clinical advice. Giving it is a red flag (S9). Declining warmly and redirecting is the top-band behaviour.

temporality.description: Governs review cadence and the current_affairs_expiry field.

values.definition: Stable for years. Ethics principles, communication skills, personal reflection.
Changes over one to three years. NHS structure, screening programmes, professional guidance.
Changes within a cycle. Industrial action, legislation in progress, published statistics, named ministers.
values.rule: Must carry a hard expiry date. Content past expiry is withheld from users, not merely flagged.
